o: A strong pair satisfies |x-y| <= min(x,y); we maximize XOR over pairs drawn from nums (reuse allowed). With n <= 50 and values <= 100, checking all O(n²) pairs is instant. Example: in [1,2,3,4,5] the pair (3,4) gives XOR 7.
k: Constraints are tiny — brute force over all pairs is intended.
Sorting lets you prune: once y > 2x no pair with that x is strong.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over all pairs
a.i: Try every ordered pair (including i == j) and keep the maximum XOR among strong pairs. Sorting first allows skipping pairs where nums[j] > 2*nums[i], though it is unnecessary at this scale.
s: Sort a copy of nums (optional pruning aid).
Double loop over all pairs (i, j).
If |a-b| <= min(a,b), update the answer with a^b.
Return the maximum found (at least 0 from pairing an element with itself).

a.n: Approach 2: Sort + sliding window with binary trie (scalable version)
a.i: Sort nums; for each right element y, the strong partners form a contiguous window [y/2, y]. Insert elements into a binary trie as the window slides and query the max XOR — this is the O(n log C · 30) pattern that generalizes to the Hard version of this problem.
s: Sort nums; maintain window [l, r] with nums[r] <= 2*nums[l].
Insert nums[r] into a binary trie of 7–30 bit paths.
Query trie for max XOR with nums[r], then advance l removing stale leaves.
a.t: O(n log n + n·B) with B ≈ 7 bits — sorting plus trie operations.

w: Brute force is the right interview answer here; present the trie version as the scalable follow-up (it solves the Hard variant with 5e4 elements and 20 bits). Pitfall: remember pairs (x, x) are strong, so the answer is at least 0.
